a-brand-new-uncle.title: A Brand-New Uncle
a-brand-new-uncle.summary: Library catalogs describe a story in which Bard Smith and his wife solve their troubles by taking in a ten-year-old uncle for their grandchildren. It is one of Seredy's last books, which she wrote and illustrated herself.
a-brand-new-uncle.note: Corrected: published 1961 (Viking), not 1941; it is not part of the Hungarian Good Master stories, so the earlier Kate, Jancsi and Hungary details were wrong.

a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.title: A Tale of Two Cities
a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.summary: In this simplified retelling of Dickens's novel, a freed Bastille prisoner, his daughter and a French exile are drawn into the dangers of London and Paris before and during the French Revolution. A London lawyer who closely resembles the exile plays a decisive part.
a-tale-of-two-cities-adapted-by-patricia.note: Original novel 1859. The adapted edition by Patricia Krapesh (also spelled Patti) was a 1991 Steck-Vaughn easy reader according to a library catalog record seen in search results; no page describing the adaptation itself could be opened.

amy-and-the-sorrel-summer.title: Amy and the Sorrel Summer
amy-and-the-sorrel-summer.summary: A children's book published in 1964 by Holt, Rinehart and Winston. No plot description could be found online.
amy-and-the-sorrel-summer.note: Existence confirmed in Open Library (1964, Holt, Rinehart and Winston; author also listed as Laura H. Fisher). Plot not verified; the earlier horse-story description was a guess.

away-goes-sally.title: Away Goes Sally
away-goes-sally.summary: Sally and her relatives set out on a winter journey from Massachusetts to Maine in a small house mounted on runners. It is the first of five historical novels about Sally.
away-goes-sally.setting: New England, a journey from Massachusetts to Maine
away-goes-sally.note: Plot sketch comes from library catalog text in search results; character names Sally Pickering and Uncle Jotham from the earlier draft could not be verified and were removed.

cat-walk.title: Cat Walk
cat-walk.summary: A young barnyard cat who wants more than a life of catching rats sets out in search of a name. His journey eventually leads him to a place he can call home.
characters: Cat — a young farm cat in search of a name
cat-walk.setting: A farm and the road beyond
cat-walk.note: Corrected: this is a farm cat on a quest, not a stray in an American town; Harper & Row, 1983.

doctor-dolittle-s-zoo.title: Doctor Dolittle's Zoo
doctor-dolittle-s-zoo.summary: Doctor Dolittle comes home from his voyages and sets his house in order, expanding his cage-free zoo with a home for crossbred dogs and a club for rodents. Much of the book is the members of the Rat and Mouse Club telling their life stories, and the Doctor also helps Kling, the Dog Detective, with a mystery.
characters: Rat and Mouse Club — storytelling rodents
doctor-dolittle-s-zoo.note: Corrected series position: fifth Dolittle book, not sixth. Earlier characters Polynesia, Jip and Dab-Dab were not confirmed for this volume.

ghosts-a-classic-collection.title: Ghosts: A Classic Collection
ghosts-a-classic-collection.summary: A collection of ghost stories. Its contents could not be confirmed.
ghosts-a-classic-collection.note: Searched the title with Ingram and Sturrock. The only trace is Open Library's illustrated ghost-story collection 'Ghosts' (Unicorn Publishing House, 1989, illustrated by Walt Sturrock, b. 1961), which may be the same book, but no record shows the subtitle or John Ingram as editor. Not confirmed.

her-majesty-grace-jones.title: Her Majesty, Grace Jones
her-majesty-grace-jones.summary: Set during the Depression, this book follows Grace Jones, a girl who imagines she is the eldest daughter of King George VI and so the future Queen of England. It was Langton's first book for children.
characters: Grace Jones — imaginative girl who believes she will be queen
her-majesty-grace-jones.note: US title is The Majesty of Grace (1961); Her Majesty, Grace Jones is an alternate title. Illustrated by Langton herself, not Emily Arnold McCully.

incognito-mosquito-private-insective.title: Incognito Mosquito, Private Insective
incognito-mosquito-private-insective.summary: A mosquito detective recounts his cases and run-ins with other insect characters to a young reporter, in a send-up of private-eye stories.
incognito-mosquito-private-insective.note: First published 1982 (Lothrop, Lee and Shepard); sequels followed in 1986 and 1987. Author's full name not found.

little-house-books-complete-set.title: Little House Books (complete set)
little-house-books-complete-set.summary: Laura Ingalls Wilder's autobiographical series follows a pioneer family from a log cabin in Wisconsin's Big Woods through Kansas, Minnesota and Dakota Territory. The books cover her childhood, her teaching years and her marriage.
characters: Laura Ingalls — the author as a girl
little-house-books-complete-set.note: Eight original books 1932-1943; the ninth, The First Four Years, appeared in 1971 and is included in many complete sets. Garth Williams illustrated the uniform edition reissued in 1953, not the originals.

midnight-is-a-place.title: Midnight Is a Place
midnight-is-a-place.summary: Two disinherited orphans, Lucas Bell and Anna-Marie, are cheated of their inheritance in a grim 19th-century mill town. When Midnight Court burns, they face child labor in the mill and a ring of extortionists.
characters: Lucas Bell — orphan who scavenges in the sewers
Anna-Marie — orphan sent to work in the mill
Sir Randolph Grimsby — owner of Midnight Court and the mill
Bludward — extortionist in a steam-driven wheelchair
midnight-is-a-place.setting: Blastburn, a fictional northern English mill town, Victorian era
midnight-is-a-place.note: Corrected: the heroine is Anna-Marie, not Lucy. A related Aiken novel set in the Wolves Chronicles world but not part of that series.

new-dawn-on-rocky-ridge.title: New Dawn on Rocky Ridge
new-dawn-on-rocky-ridge.summary: A volume in the Rocky Ridge Years series about Rose Wilder, Laura Ingalls Wilder's daughter, growing up in the Ozarks. Its individual plot could not be confirmed.
characters: Rose Wilder — Laura Ingalls Wilder's daughter
new-dawn-on-rocky-ridge.note: Corrected: published 1997 (Open Library and Wikipedia agree), not 1994.

out-of-the-silent-planet.title: Out of the Silent Planet
out-of-the-silent-planet.summary: Cambridge philologist Ransom is drugged and carried by spaceship to Malacandra, which is Mars. Escaping his captors, he learns the languages and customs of its three intelligent peoples and meets the planet's spirit ruler.

redwall-series.title: Redwall series
redwall-series.summary: In Jacques's long-running fantasy series, mice, badgers, hares and other woodland creatures defend Redwall Abbey and Mossflower Wood from vermin such as rats, weasels and stoats. Each book is mostly self-contained.
characters: Cluny the Scourge — villainous rat warlord
Martin the Warrior — legendary mouse hero
redwall-series.note: Volumes listed: Redwall 1986, Mossflower 1988, Mattimeo 1989, Mariel of Redwall 1991, Salamandastron 1992, Martin the Warrior 1993. Illustrator not confirmed.

see-inside-an-egyptian-town.title: See Inside an Egyptian Town
see-inside-an-egyptian-town.summary: An illustrated look at the buildings and daily life of an ancient Egyptian town founded in 1375 B.C. to honor the god Aten. It belongs to Unstead's See Inside series for young readers.
see-inside-an-egyptian-town.note: Corrected: first edition 1977 (Hutchinson, London; Warwick Press edition 1978), not 1969.

smith-of-wootton-major-farmer-giles-of-h.title: Smith of Wootton Major & Farmer Giles of Ham
smith-of-wootton-major-farmer-giles-of-h.summary: Two short Tolkien tales in one volume. In Farmer Giles of Ham a reluctant farmer becomes a dragon-taming hero, and in Smith of Wootton Major a village smith swallows a star that opens the way into Faery.
characters: Smith (Starbrow) — village smith who enters Faery
smith-of-wootton-major-farmer-giles-of-h.setting: Rural England of an imagined past
smith-of-wootton-major-farmer-giles-of-h.note: Farmer Giles of Ham 1949; Smith of Wootton Major 1967; the paired edition appeared from Ballantine in 1969.

tecwyn-the-last-of-the-welsh-dragons.title: Tecwyn, the Last of the Welsh Dragons
tecwyn-the-last-of-the-welsh-dragons.summary: A fire-breathing dragon, the last of his kind, hatches in the Welsh town of Pennyben and puts a strain on the town's coal supply.
tecwyn-the-last-of-the-welsh-dragons.note: Identified: Parents' Magazine Press, New York, 1967.

the-alley.title: The Alley
the-alley.summary: Twenty-six families live in a self-contained alley of houses on a college campus, and their thirty-three children have their own society. When the Ives family is burgled, the children take over the investigation and stage a mock trial.
the-alley.setting: An alley of houses on a college campus
the-alley.note: Corrected: the setting is a campus alley with a burglary, not a Cranbury street; the earlier plot guess was wrong. Harcourt, Brace & World, 1964.

the-blood-and-thunder-adventure-on-hurri.title: The Blood-and-Thunder Adventure on Hurricane Peak
the-blood-and-thunder-adventure-on-hurri.summary: The students of the Unexpected School on Hurricane Peak set out to foil the wicked Sir Quincey and his accomplices while solving several mysteries along the way.
the-blood-and-thunder-adventure-on-hurri.note: Published by J. M. Dent in 1989; the US edition came from McElderry. Summary from a library abstract in search results.

the-case-of-the-frightened-friend.title: The Case of the Frightened Friend
the-case-of-the-frightened-friend.summary: Andrew and Inspector Wyatt help a friend whose father has died mysteriously, whose grandfather is an invalid and whose stepmother behaves suspiciously around the doctor. The case is also tied to a retired admiral and an intelligence leak.
the-case-of-the-frightened-friend.note: Corrected: the hero is Andrew Tillett, not Tolliver; published 1984 (Atheneum), not 1973.

the-case-of-the-watching-boy.title: The Case of the Watching Boy
the-case-of-the-watching-boy.summary: Andrew Tillett helps a younger classmate return an abducted boy to his mother. When police report a local kidnapping, Andrew and his friends trace the case to London's upper class.
the-case-of-the-watching-boy.note: Corrected: the hero is Andrew Tillett, not Tolliver; published 1987 (Atheneum), not 1975. Series number from a catalog summary.

the-dandelion-caper.title: The Dandelion Caper
the-dandelion-caper.summary: Walter and his friend Kathy have helped many stranded space tourists, and now they face evil aliens in an abandoned house. A cat with unusual powers comes to their aid.
characters: Walter — boy who helps stranded aliens
the-dandelion-caper.note: Published 1986 by Putnam; the earlier 'puzzling affair involving dandelions' draft was wrong.

the-enchanter-s-spell-five-famous-tales.title: The Enchanter's Spell: Five Famous Tales
the-enchanter-s-spell-five-famous-tales.summary: Spirin retells and illustrates five famous tales: Little Daylight, The Princess and the Seven Brothers, The Nutcracker, The Beautiful Kitchen Maid and The Emperor's New Clothes. Each gets its own period setting in his paintings.

the-giant.title: The Giant
the-giant.summary: An eight-year-old boy is seven stories tall because he has a perfect digestive system. His family and friends try to hide him, so the narrator befriends him and plans a way for him to live openly.
the-giant.note: Identified as the Viking Press 1954 book; the vague earlier summary was replaced.

the-island-on-bird-street.title: The Island on Bird Street
the-island-on-bird-street.summary: Eleven-year-old Alex, a Jewish boy in a ghetto in occupied Poland, is separated from his father when deportations begin. Alone in a bombed-out building, he must find food and avoid soldiers while he waits for his father to return.
the-island-on-bird-street.setting: A ghetto in occupied Poland, World War II
the-island-on-bird-street.note: Hebrew original 1981 (Keter); English translation by Hillel Halkin, 1984.

the-lord-of-the-rings.title: The Lord of the Rings
the-lord-of-the-rings.summary: Frodo Baggins and his companions set out to destroy a ring forged by the Dark Lord Sauron by casting it into Mount Doom. The story was published in three volumes: The Fellowship of the Ring, The Two Towers and The Return of the King.

the-mysterious-disappearance-of-leon-i-m.title: The Mysterious Disappearance of Leon (I Mean Noel)
the-mysterious-disappearance-of-leon-i-m.summary: Caroline Fish Carillon searches for her husband Leon, who now goes by Noel and vanished after shouting a garbled message while falling overboard from a boat. She spends years decoding it with her adopted twins and an old friend, in a story packed with word puzzles.
characters: Caroline Fish Carillon — the searching wife
Tony and Tina — her adopted twins
the-mysterious-disappearance-of-leon-i-m.note: Corrected: the heroine is Caroline Fish Carillon, not Ellen. Dutton, 1971; illustrator not confirmed.

the-pet-sitting-peril.title: The Pet-Sitting Peril
the-pet-sitting-peril.summary: A boy who does odd jobs in an apartment house, including pet-sitting, gets mixed up with arsonists working for the building's owner. The owner plans to burn it down for the insurance.

the-shepherd-moon.title: The Shepherd Moon
the-shepherd-moon.summary: A colonist from a forgotten artificial moon returns to Earth in the far future. A thirteen-year-old girl named Merry and her grandfather work to protect their culture from the visitor's unusual powers.
characters: Her grandfather — protector of their way of life
the-shepherd-moon.note: Corrected: the heroine is Merry, not Meg. Subtitled A Novel of the Future; Viking, 1984.

the-summer-of-the-falcon.title: The Summer of the Falcon
the-summer-of-the-falcon.summary: June Pritchard, thirteen, is given a sparrow hawk to train as a pet. The bird, Zander, resists new rules as stubbornly as June does.
the-summer-of-the-falcon.setting: A family summer house in the mountains
the-summer-of-the-falcon.note: Corrected: Zander is the bird, not her brother. Crowell, 1962; plot from a library description seen in search results.

the-thunder-pup.title: The Thunder-Pup
the-thunder-pup.summary: A 1981 children's novel by Janet Hickman about a dog. No plot description could be found online.
the-thunder-pup.note: Book exists (Open Library, subject Dogs, Fiction); the plot in the earlier draft could not be verified and was removed.

the-white-archer-an-eskimo-legend.title: The White Archer: An Eskimo Legend
the-white-archer-an-eskimo-legend.summary: A young Inuit sets out to avenge his parents' violent deaths and spends years becoming a master archer. Over that time he outgrows his hatred.
awards: Canadian Library Association Book of the Year for Children (1968)
the-white-archer-an-eskimo-legend.note: Harcourt, Brace & World, 1967. Houston wrote and illustrated it.

tiger-burning-bright.title: Tiger Burning Bright
tiger-burning-bright.summary: A book by Theodora Du Bois listed in Open Library for 1963. No plot description could be found.
tiger-burning-bright.note: Not Peter Feibleman's play Tiger, Tiger, Burning Bright (1963). Wikipedia dates the Du Bois book 1964 but Open Library gives 1963; genre and plot unconfirmed.

wild-trek.title: Wild Trek
wild-trek.summary: Trapper Link Stevens and his half-wild snow dog Chiri set out to rescue a naturalist stranded in the Caribou Mountains. They face a cougar, hostile wolves and the wilderness itself.
wild-trek.note: Corrected: the characters are Link Stevens and Chiri, not Jim and Chinook. Holiday House, 1950.

C. S. Lewis.bio: Lewis taught English literature at Oxford and then Cambridge. A close friend of J. R. R. Tolkien, he belonged to the Inklings literary group. His Christian radio talks and fiction made him widely read.

Margaret Mahy.bio: Mahy was a New Zealand librarian who became a prolific children's and young-adult author. She won the Carnegie Medal twice and received the Hans Christian Andersen Award in 2006. Her stories often have supernatural touches but focus on growing up.

Hugh Lofting.bio: Lofting trained as a civil engineer and served in the Irish Guards in World War I. He created Doctor Dolittle in illustrated letters to his children from the trenches. The Voyages of Doctor Dolittle won the Newbery Medal.

known_for: A Tale of Two Cities (simplified adaptation)

Eleanor Estes.bio: Estes was a children's librarian who began writing while recovering from tuberculosis. Her Connecticut childhood and small-town family life inspired many of her twenty books. She won the Newbery Medal for Ginger Pye.

Kate Seredy.bio: Seredy trained as an art teacher in Budapest and moved to the United States in 1922. She wrote and illustrated her own books and saw herself first as an illustrator. The White Stag won the Newbery Medal.

Gennady Spirin.bio: Spirin is a Russian painter and children's book illustrator known for his watercolor style. He studied in Moscow and moved to the United States after the Soviet Union dissolved, settling in Princeton, New Jersey. He illustrated many fairy tales and classic stories.

Laura Ingalls Wilder.bio: Wilder grew up in pioneer families in Wisconsin, Kansas, Minnesota and Dakota Territory and became a teacher. She began writing children's books in her sixties, encouraged by her daughter Rose Wilder Lane. Her Little House series drew on her own childhood.
known_for: Little House in the Big Woods

Theodora Du Bois.bio: Theodora Du Bois, born Theodora McCormick, wrote mysteries, children's books, romances and science fiction. She married engineer Delafield Du Bois in 1918. Her publisher dropped her after her 1954 novel Seeing Red criticized the House Un-American Activities Committee.

Mary Stolz.bio: Stolz, born Mary Slattery, began writing in the late 1940s when arthritis kept her housebound. She wrote fiction for children and young adults, mostly for Harper. She earned Newbery Honors for Belling the Tiger and The Noonday Friends.

Ellen Raskin.bio: Raskin worked as a commercial artist in New York and designed more than a thousand book jackets, including the first edition of A Wrinkle in Time. She then turned to writing and illustrating her own picture books and puzzle mysteries. The Westing Game won the Newbery Medal.
known_for: The Mysterious Disappearance of Leon (I Mean Noel)

R. J. Unstead.bio: Robert John Unstead was a teacher who became headmaster of a primary school in Letchworth. He wrote or edited over forty illustrated history books for young readers, some selling in the millions. He served in the RAF in World War II.

Jim Kjelgaard.bio: Kjelgaard grew up on a farm in Pennsylvania's Allegheny Mountains and wrote more than forty novels, mostly about dogs and wild animals. He also sold short fiction to magazines such as The Saturday Evening Post. Big Red became a 1962 Disney film.

Willo Davis Roberts.bio: Roberts was known mainly for children's mystery and suspense novels. She began with adult fiction in the 1950s and published her first children's book in 1975. She won the Edgar Allan Poe Award for juvenile mysteries in 1989, 1995 and 1997.
known_for: The View from the Cherry Tree
The Girl with the Silver Eyes

Gene DeWeese.bio: Thomas Eugene DeWeese worked as an electronics technician and technical writer in Milwaukee before freelancing full time in 1974. He wrote more than forty books across science fiction, mystery and young-adult fiction. He is best known for his Star Trek novels.
known_for: The Adventures of a Two-Minute Werewolf

Joan Aiken.bio: Aiken was the daughter of the American poet Conrad Aiken and was mostly taught at home. She wrote children's alternative-history novels, supernatural stories, thrillers and Jane Austen continuations. She received an MBE in 1999 for services to children's literature.

Elizabeth Coatsworth.bio: Coatsworth was a poet and author who graduated from Vassar and later lived in Maine. She published over ninety books and married writer Henry Beston in 1929. She won the Newbery Medal for The Cat Who Went to Heaven.
known_for: The Cat Who Went to Heaven

Jane Langton.bio: Langton studied astronomy and art history and lived near Concord, Massachusetts. She wrote and illustrated children's fantasies and the Homer Kelly mystery series. The Fledgling was a Newbery Honor book, and she received an Edgar Grand Master award in 2018.

Robert Newman.bio: Robert Newman wrote children's mystery novels for Atheneum, including the Andrew Tillett series. The listings found give his dates as 1909-1988 but few other details.
known_for: The Case of the Baker Street Irregular
The Case of the Frightened Friend
The Case of the Watching Boy

William Pène du Bois.bio: Pène du Bois was educated partly in France and wrote and illustrated children's books. He was a founding editor and art editor of The Paris Review. The Twenty-One Balloons won the 1948 Newbery Medal.

Brian Jacques.bio: Jacques worked as a sailor, truck driver, bus driver and milkman before writing. He wrote the first Redwall book for blind children at a Liverpool school where he delivered milk. He hosted a BBC Radio Merseyside show for twenty years.

James Houston.bio: Houston spent about twelve years in the Canadian Arctic and helped develop Inuit printmaking. He later moved to New York to work for Steuben Glass. He wrote and illustrated children's books and adult novels about Arctic life.

Janet Hickman.bio: Janet Hickman is credited in Open Library with several children's novels from the 1970s to the 2000s. Few personal details could be confirmed.

Uri Orlev.bio: Orlev survived the Warsaw Ghetto and Bergen-Belsen as a child and emigrated to Israel after the war. He became a full-time children's writer and translator in 1968. He won the Hans Christian Andersen Award in 1996.
known_for: The Man from the Other Side

Jean Craighead George.bio: George grew up in a family of naturalists and worked as a Washington Post reporter. She wrote more than a hundred books for young readers, often about the natural world. Julie of the Wolves won the Newbery Medal.

known_for: Incognito Mosquito Takes to the Air
Tecwyn, the Last of the Welsh Dragons

J. R. R. Tolkien.birthplace: Bloemfontein, Orange Free State (now South Africa)
J. R. R. Tolkien.bio: Tolkien was an Oxford philologist and professor of Anglo-Saxon and later of English language and literature. A devout Catholic and close friend of C. S. Lewis, he created Middle-earth. He was made a CBE in 1972.

H. M. Hoover.bio: Helen Mary Hoover wrote science fiction and other novels mainly for older children from 1969 to 1996. Her stories often explore friendships between people of different generations. She lived for many years in Virginia.

Charles Dickens.bio: Dickens left school at twelve to work in a boot-blacking factory when his father was jailed for debt. He became a journalist and then the most popular novelist of Victorian England. His serialized novels brought him international fame.

Roger Lea MacBride.bio: MacBride was a lawyer and politician who served one term in the Vermont House and was the Libertarian presidential nominee in 1976. He inherited the literary estate of Rose Wilder Lane and went on to write the Rocky Ridge Years books about her childhood. He died in Miami Beach.
